title: Geniva
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: He was a great man in Rav’s days, as in Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah, chapter 2, end of halakhah 8: a dispute of Rav and Geniva, and Rav said of him: “I am an elder and he is an elder.” Hyman nevertheless argues that he was Rav’s student and that Rav said this only out of humility, as we find in Berakhot 25a, “Geniva said that Rav said”; in Avodah Zarah 36b, in Rav’s name; and in Berakhot 27a, “Rav visited Geniva’s house.” We likewise find in Chullin: “Geniva said that Rav Assi said.”

He had a dispute with Mar Ukva, as in Gittin 7a, where Mar Ukva sent to Rabbi Elazar (in the Land of Israel): “People stand against me, and it is in my power to hand them over to the government — what is the law?” He sent to him: “Be silent before the Lord” … The thing came forth from Rabbi Elazar’s mouth, and they put Geniva in a neck-iron. Hyman suggests that apparently he was then acquitted, as in Gittin 31b: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda were sitting; Geniva passed by them. One said to the other, “Let us rise before him, for he is a learned man.” The other said to him, “Shall we rise before a quarrelsome man?” (Rashi explains: because of the incident with Mar Ukva and Rabbi Elazar.) Meanwhile he came to them … he said to them: “Thus said Rav Chanan bar Rava that Rav said,” etc.

A halakhah of his is likewise mentioned in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot, chapter 6, end of halakhah 6: “Geniva said: Oil for [removing] dirt requires no blessing”; in Jerusalem Talmud Beitzah 2:8: “Geniva said: The halakhah,” etc.; in Bereshit Rabbah 10:9, a dispute of Geniva and the Rabbis; and in Kohelet Rabbah 5:14, “Geniva said: [A parable of] a fox that found a vineyard,” etc. Of those who speak in his name Hyman finds only, in Chullin 44a, “Ravina (Rabbi Avina) said that Geniva said”; there, 50b, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: “It was explained to me by Geniva himself at the ferry of Nehardea”; and in Berakhot 25a: “Geniva said that Rav said — Rav Yosef said: May his Master forgive Geniva.” His end was as had come forth from Rabbi Elazar’s mouth, as in Gittin 65b: Geniva was going out in a neck-iron (to be executed by the government; and so it is explicit in Jerusalem Talmud Gittin 7:5, “Geniva was taken out to be killed”). As he was going out he said: “Give four hundred zuz to Rabbi Avina” (the book Chikrei Lev, p. 2, says that this is Rabbi Avina, Rav Ashi’s colleague, and Hyman respectfully rejects that identification as a grave error). Rabbi Zeira said: “Let Rabbi Avina go to Rav Huna his teacher.” Hyman considers it very likely that he gave it to Rabbi Avina because he was the one who was Geniva’s student and spoke in his name, as cited above.

notes.text: ב״א העומדים is read people standing against me, and Chullin lacks a locator for the Assi chain. Hyman’s humility interpretation, acquittal conjecture, Avina identification and later execution remain attributed; only in his name preserves his limited surviving-record claim, not a new corpus absence assertion.

The consulted Gittin 31b names Geniva in the learned-man/quarrelsome-man exchange. That incident alone does not prove Hyman’s acquittal conjecture. His humility explanation, later execution, Avina identification and restricted surviving-record claim remain attributed, and the defective Chikrei Lev page is not silently repaired.
